title: Shakuntala at court
hookLine: Shakuntala walks into the king's hall with his son, he says he's never seen her, and she answers with an old verse
carry: a child is your own self, born again
last: MARRIAGE BY YOUR OWN CHOICE HAS A PLACE IN DHARMA.

cards: A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son.
Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching.

teach.b: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once. Then she speaks, for a long time.
Here is some of it, in paraphrase.

teach.h: THE SUN AND MOON WERE WITNESSES
teach.b: First, witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him, but the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. Then the boy.

teach.h: YOU ARE MY OWN SELF, CALLED SON
teach.b: She reminds the king of an old Vedic verse: from my limbs you are born, from my heart you arise; you are my own self, called son.

When the king answers with insults about her mother and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around: you see others' faults as small as a mustard seed, and miss your own, as big as a bilva fruit. She never begs.

teach.h: A VOICE FROM THE SKY AGREES
teach.b: Then a voice from the sky tells the king she speaks the truth, and the boy is his. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. Here's the teaching.
That verse is older than the story. In the Vedic household rites, a father says it over his newborn, and again when he comes home from a journey and breathes in the scent of his child's head.
In Hindu thought, a child isn't a possession or a stranger.

teach.h: A CHILD IS YOUR OWN SELF, BORN AGAIN.
teach.b: A child is your own self, born again, and no father can say he doesn't know his own self.
Plenty of Hindu parents and grandparents still greet a child by breathing in the top of their head, whether or not they know the verse. The old rite ends with a blessing: live a hundred autumns.

how: Hindus know Shakuntala's speech at court from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva; the same story is retold in the poet Kalidasa's later play, which changes how the king comes to forget her.

o: a wife who reminded a denying king his son was his own self
a wife who begged a king in tears to take her back
a wife who left the hall in silence, never to return

games.q: Shakuntala at court — tap the pairs.

witnesses to what the king did
'you are my own self, called son'
the old verse she reminds him of
the faults he sees in others
the faults he can't see in himself

s: Shakuntala begged the king to take her back
she never begs: she tells him the truth about himself, then turns to go.
in the epic, a voice from the sky tells the king the boy is his
only then does Dushyanta take Shakuntala and his son in.
the verse she recites belongs to old Hindu household rites
a father says it over his newborn, and on coming home from a journey.

games.q: you're Shakuntala, in the king's hall, holding your son's hand. the king says he has never seen you before. what do you say?
o: nothing; leave quietly so as not to shame him.
remind him of the old verse: this boy is your own self, born again.
fall at his feet and beg.
games.why: she names the witnesses and reminds him of the verse: you are my own self, called son. when he still refuses, a voice from the sky confirms her.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is part of you: a child, a niece or nephew, a younger cousin, or the person who first held you that way.
Picture the old greeting, breathing in the top of their head, and on each out-breath say inwardly: you are part of me. If you pray, you can bless them the way the rite does: live a hundred autumns.

wordCard.voice: Shakuntala. The woman who stood in a king's hall and reminded him that his son was his own self, until the sky itself agreed.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the epic explains her name from shakunta, bird, for the birds that guarded her as a baby.

carryVoice: Your line: a child is your own self, born again. Shakuntala made a king remember it. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Shakuntala at Dushyanta's court; his denial; her speech: the witnesses, the verse 'from my limbs you are born… you are my own self, called son', the son as a mirror, the mustard seed and the bilva fruit; the king's insults; the voice from the sky)
Kaushitaki Upanishad, ch. 2 (the father, back from a journey, smells his son's head and says 'from my limbs you are born…'; section numbering varies); Grihya Sutras (the birth rite)
